analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers and public programs to cover HIV prevention drugs with no cost to patients.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required free coverage of HIV prevention medication across private and public insurance, died in committee without a vote after gaining 30 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, the VA, and TRICARE to cover drugs that prevent HIV, plus the lab tests and clinic visits that go with them, with no copays, deductibles, or preapproval hurdles. It would have barred life, disability, and long-term care insurers from penalizing people simply for taking HIV prevention medication. It also would have funded PrEP and PEP for people without adequate insurance and paid for public education campaigns.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.1 million Americans who could benefit from HIV prevention medication gain the most, especially gay and bisexual men, transgender women, and Black and Latino people, who the bill's findings say are diagnosed at far higher rates and prescribed PrEP at far lower rates than white patients (8% of eligible Black Americans versus 63% of eligible white Americans in 2019). People with private insurance would pay nothing for the drugs and related care; Medicaid, Medicare, CHIP, VA, and TRICARE beneficiaries would get the same; and uninsured or underinsured people would be reached through new federal grants. Anyone denied life, disability, or long-term care insurance for taking PrEP would gain legal protection.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of HIV, especially uninsured and people of color

how_it_helps.text: Requires private health plans to cover all FDA-approved HIV prevention drugs, plus lab tests, clinic visits, and administrative fees, with zero cost-sharing and no preauthorization, effective for plan years starting January 1, 2023.

Extends the same free coverage to Medicare (waiving Part B deductible and coinsurance and eliminating Part D cost-sharing for prevention drugs), Medicaid, CHIP, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, VA care, and TRICARE.

Makes it unlawful for life, disability, or long-term care insurers to deny coverage, limit benefits, or raise premiums because someone takes HIV prevention medication, and gives patients a private right of action with attorney fees to enforce their rights.

Creates a grant program for states, territories, tribes, and community clinics to provide PrEP and PEP to uninsured and underinsured people, and funds CDC public and provider education campaigns aimed at the communities where the drugs are most underused.

Directs HHS to update privacy rules so a person can use these benefits under a family plan without the policyholder being told, protecting people whose safety or family situation makes confidentiality critical.

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on health insurers, whose premiums would absorb the price of free PrEP drugs and related services, and on federal and state budgets, since Medicaid, Medicare, CHIP, VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service must cover these services without cost-sharing and the grant and education programs are authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' through fiscal 2028. Brand-name drug makers gain sales volume but could face pressure as plans steer toward therapeutically equivalent drugs to avoid the preauthorization exemption.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, Medicare/Medicaid budgets, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds costs for insurers and public programs. PrEP drugs can cost around $1,700 to $2,000 a month at brand prices, so requiring coverage of the drugs plus all related lab work and visits with no patient cost-sharing raises premiums and federal health spending, and the bill's spending authorizations are open-ended with no dollar cap.

The preauthorization ban has a carve-out that lets plans require approval for one brand-name drug so long as they cover a therapeutically equivalent drug without it, which could steer some patients to older generic PrEP rather than newer options like the long-acting injectable the bill's findings note was under FDA review.

The bill leans on annual appropriations for its grant and education programs, which are authorized at unspecified sums for fiscal 2023 through 2028; the coverage mandates are guaranteed but the programs for the uninsured are only as strong as future appropriations.
The prohibition on insurance discrimination is enforced only by state insurance regulators, whose powers vary, so protection could be uneven across states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and well-targeted: daily PrEP cuts the risk of getting HIV from sex by about 99%, yet only 23% of the roughly 1.1 million people who could benefit filled a prescription in 2019, with stark racial gaps. Freeing the drug, the lab work, and the clinic visits of all patient costs directly attacks the main documented barriers. The main costs are higher premiums and public health spending, though preventing HIV infection is far cheaper than a lifetime of treatment, and the carve-out for brand-name drugs and reliance on annual appropriations blunt parts of the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the PrEP Access and Coverage Act on December 1, 2021, joined by Senator Amy Klobuchar.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
It gathered 30 cosponsors — 29 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents — all from one side of the aisle.
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the Senate floor, and the full action history shows no activity after the initial referral.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and bills that were not passed expire and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, life and disability insurers, and brand-name drug pricing arrangements were left untouched, since the bill never advanced; the roughly 1.1 million people who could benefit from PrEP gained nothing, and the documented racial gaps in PrEP access persisted through the end of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and drug makers; PrEP users gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats or the independents who caucus with them; no Republican senator signed on, and the bill never reached a roll-call vote.

industries.note: The bill forces private plans to cover HIV prevention drugs, lab work, and follow-up visits with zero patient cost-sharing and no preauthorization, moving those costs onto premiums. The industry already faced a similar requirement for most plans under existing preventive-care rules, so this extends and hardens it.

industries.industry: Life, disability, and long-term care insurers
industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to deny, limit, or reprice these policies because someone takes HIV prevention medication, removing an underwriting lever, and lets patients sue with attorney fees.

Mandated free coverage and a new grant program for the uninsured expand the customer base for PrEP drugs. But the preauthorization exemption lets plans require approval for one brand-name drug if they cover a therapeutically equivalent one without it, pushing utilization toward generics.

industries.industry: Community health centers and HIV service organizations
industries.note: Federally qualified health centers, rural clinics, family planning grantees, and community organizations become eligible for direct federal grants to deliver PrEP and PEP to uninsured people.
